title: Christian Bookstore Agent
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Question ID: 14701_christian_bookstore_agent

Lydia was fired by Peter, the director of a private Christian bookstore. Lydia wanted revenge against Peter, but decided against trying to do it herself because she knew Peter was protected by private security guards whenever he was at the store.

Lydia knew that Stephen had a violent temper and was very jealous. Lydia falsely told Stephen that Stephen’s wife, Ruth, was having an affair with Peter. Enraged, Stephen said, “What am I going to do?” Lydia replied, “If it were my spouse, I’d walk into Peter’s office and shoot him.”

Stephen grabbed a revolver and rushed to the bookstore. He walked into the bookstore carrying the gun in his hand. One of the security guards, believing a robbery was about to occur, shot and killed Stephen.

If charged with attempted murder of Peter, Lydia should be found:
call: If charged with attempted murder of Peter, Lydia should be found:

choices.A: Guilty, because Lydia intended to kill Peter and used Stephen to carry out her plan.
choices.B: Guilty, because Lydia was extremely reckless as to Peter.
choices.C: Not guilty, because Peter was never in imminent danger of being killed.
choices.D: Not guilty, because Stephen, if successful, would be guilty of no more than manslaughter and an accessory cannot be guilty of a higher crime than the principal.

rightExplanation:
A is correct.

Gold Key: Attempted murder requires the intent to kill plus a substantial step toward killing. Extreme recklessness is not enough. A substantial step can be using, urging, or manipulating another person to carry out the killing.

Silver Key: Do not ask whether Peter was actually reached. The call is attempted murder by the instigator. Lock the instigator’s mental state and the instigator’s step.

Lydia wanted Peter killed. She chose Stephen because she knew he was violent and jealous. She lied to trigger Stephen’s jealousy, then gave him the killing script. Stephen armed himself and went to Peter’s workplace. That leaves A as the true and responsive answer.

wrongExplanations.B: It keeps the guilty outcome but swaps the mental state. Gold Key: attempt is not an extreme-recklessness crime. The answer must say intent to kill, not merely risk creation.
wrongExplanations.C: It invents a danger-zone requirement. Silver Key: the fact that the guard stopped Stephen goes to completion, not attempt. Attempt asks whether the instigator took a substantial step with the required intent.
wrongExplanations.D: It caps Lydia’s guilt by Stephen’s likely mitigation. Gold Key: the instigator/helper can be judged by her own mental state. Stephen’s possible manslaughter mitigation does not automatically reduce Lydia’s own attempted-murder liability.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: wrong mental-state answer. It says “extremely reckless.” The Gold Key requires intent to kill for attempted murder.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: fabricated threshold. It says Peter was never in imminent danger. The Gold Key asks substantial step, not actual danger arrival.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: absolute cap. It says an accessory cannot be guilty of a higher crime than the principal. The Gold Key says the instigator’s own mens rea controls.

c3.label: Residual
c3.text: A. No CLASH remains after anchor-assisted CUT.

studentScript: Attempted murder call. Lydia wanted Peter killed. She did not merely risk harm; she picked Stephen, lied to him, gave him the shooting script, and he went armed to Peter's store. Cut B: recklessness. Cut C: no-danger completion trap. Cut D: accessory-cap overclaim. A remains.

A.signal: A is the only answer that states intent to kill plus use of Stephen as the instrument.
A.lawyer: Attempt liability can rest on purposeful conduct constituting a substantial step; conduct designed to aid another can be attempt even if the other person does not complete the offense.

B.signal: The answer says reckless, while the Gold Key says attempted murder requires intent to kill.
B.lawyer: Extreme recklessness is not enough for attempted murder; attempt requires the target intent for the attempted homicide.

C.signal: The call asks attempt; the answer demands actual imminent danger.
C.lawyer: A substantial step is enough; factual impossibility or interruption before actual danger does not defeat attempt.

D.signal: The answer says an accessory cannot be guilty of a higher crime; the Gold Key says the helper's own mens rea can matter.
D.lawyer: The instigator/helper can be more culpable than the direct actor when the helper has the higher mens rea and the direct actor has a personal mitigation.

goldKeys.statement: Attempted murder requires intent to kill plus a substantial step; extreme recklessness is not enough. Manipulating another person to go carry out the killing can be the substantial step.
goldKeys.trigger: Instigator wants target killed, sends/uses another person, and completion is interrupted.
goldKeys.authority: Model Penal Code § 5.01; First Circuit attempt instruction commentary

goldKeys.statement: A helper or instigator is judged by that person's own mental state; the direct actor's personal mitigation does not automatically cap the helper's liability.
goldKeys.trigger: Direct actor may have heat-of-passion mitigation, but instigator planned a killing.

silverKeys.statement: On an attempt-by-instigator array, sort first by the instigator's mens rea and step; do not let failure to reach the victim answer the wrong question.
silverKeys.trigger: Guilty/not guilty split with intent, recklessness, no-danger, and accessory-cap reasons.
silverKeys.unlocks: 2 yes / 2 no array where the traps swap intent, completion, and principal-liability cap.

remediation.title: Attempt by using another person
remediation.signal: Defendant wants crime done but routes it through another person.
remediation.studentMove: Ask for the defendant's intent and the defendant's step. Then ask whether the wrong answer is demanding completion.
remediation.tinyRule: Attempt = intent + substantial step; no completed harm required.
remediation.trap: Recklessness, no imminent danger, or principal's lesser crime.
